content.summary: The written small-rank, isolation and B4 arguments justify their advertised arbitrary-support scope. R16 maximality, combined with the imported guarded classification, exhausts the complete-link alternatives of sizes 17-20. Independent bounded set checks support the isolation and maximality mechanisms. No necessary revision arose; this does not replay the imported R16 proof trees.

checks.scope: Small-rank bounds and maximum-degree root selection
checks.method: Read pinned paper/main.tex, lines 188-269, reconstructing the graph classification and degree-count proof; checked the revised manuscript Section 5.2 against R15-rho6-finite-closure.md, lines 21-28.
checks.observation: An SF2 graph has maximum degree and matching number at most two; five edges give C5 or a triangle plus a two-edge path, and six give two triangles. For an intersecting SF3 family, the degree-six case permits only six triples, while a degree-five root confines the remaining triples through three-covers. The degree-sum/intersection equations exclude maximum degree four at sizes eight and nine without a support assumption; an independent enumeration of those bounded degree-count equations found no admissible states. The revised maximum-degree root choice correctly supplies global cap five only when degree six is absent.

checks.scope: P-type support isolation and Q8 core isolation
checks.method: Reconstructed pinned main.tex, lines 272-305, and independently tested candidate extensions with literal sunflower witnesses, allowing three fresh labels for one possible new triple.
checks.observation: Across all 56 zero/one/two-block deletions of P10, all 4,188 tested additional triples meeting its support were blocked except the deleted blocks themselves. For Q8, 102 tested additional triples meeting its core left exactly {0,5,6} and {1,5,6}, the hub-plus-two-leaf exceptions. Three fresh labels cover every single-extension intersection pattern; this is not an ambient-support restriction on the whole family. The results match the pair-saturation and point-link matching arguments.

checks.scope: B4 separation and the universal SF3 cap
checks.method: Read pinned main.tex, lines 308-350, and checked the actual-anchor and exceptional-block steps directly.
checks.observation: The disjoint class of an actual anchor is intersecting. When it has at least eight members, P-type deleted blocks and Q8 exceptional hub-plus-leaf blocks are themselves disjoint from the anchor, so cannot enter its complementary neighbourhood. P-type support avoidance or Q8 core avoidance then makes two disjoint neighbourhood members impossible. The universal neighbourhood bound 1+3*3+3*1=13 ensures that a hypothetical SF3 family of size at least 21 has at least eight disjoint members; B4 and the intersecting bound give total at most 20. This chain precedes R16 and uses no mu41, mu42 or SF4 size assumption.

checks.scope: R16 maximality and exhaustive complete links at sizes 17-20
checks.method: Read pinned main.tex, lines 443-462 and 612-635; reconstructed the hereditary-rho argument and both placements of a P-type part relative to the anchor. Independently tested all 270 possible extra triples on the ten R16 points plus three fresh labels.
checks.observation: Every tested extra triple has an actual two-member sunflower witness. The ordinary proof explains why: saturated hub links force avoidance of all hubs, saturated triad pairs allow at most one point per triad, and two old triples then avoid the newcomer and each other. If a 17-20 family had rho<=7, any sixteen-member subfamily would be the imported R16 and could not extend. Otherwise B4 gives two intersecting parts of sizes at most ten, yielding exactly 10+7 or 9+8; 10+8 or 9+9; 10+9; and 10+10. A P9/P10 part exists in every case. If it is the disjoint class, deleted blocks also avoid the anchor; if it is the neighbourhood, deleted blocks meet its anchor. Isolation therefore forces disjoint supports in either placement. The R16 classification itself retains its explicitly imported finite-proof dependency.
